subject: Mathematics

unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 8! You already know how to add and subtract whole numbers with confidence. In this unit you will take those skills much further and learn to add and subtract decimal numbers and fractions accurately, even when they look awkward. These are the operations that grown-ups reach for every single day, often without noticing. When Amina works out the change from a 500-shilling note at the Hargeisa market, when Yusuf measures how much water is left in a jerrycan, or when Halima adds up parts of a recipe for iftar during Ramadan, they are all adding and subtracting with decimals and fractions.

Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, activities and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

outcomes: Add and subtract decimal numbers using correct place value alignment.
Use trailing zeros so numbers with different numbers of decimal places line up.
Borrow (regroup) correctly across a decimal point in subtraction.
Estimate the answer first to check that your result is reasonable.
Find a common denominator and add or subtract fractions with different denominators.
Add and subtract mixed numbers, including when borrowing one whole is needed.
Simplify answers and convert between improper fractions and mixed numbers.
Add and subtract decimals mentally using known number facts, place value, and rounding-and-adjusting strategies.

concepts.title: Decimal Place Value
concepts.explanation:
A decimal number is simply an extension of the place value system you already know. Just as whole numbers have ones, tens and hundreds, the places to the right of the decimal point show parts of a whole. Each place is ten times smaller than the one before it: the first place is tenths (1/10), the second is hundredths (1/100), and the third is thousandths (1/1000).

Let us read the number 6.075 carefully. The 6 is in the ones place. The 0 is in the tenths place, so it means zero tenths. The 7 is in the hundredths place, so it means 7 hundredths. The 5 is in the thousandths place, so it means 5 thousandths. Putting the parts together, 6.075 = 6 + 0.07 + 0.005. Understanding what each digit is worth is the whole key to adding and subtracting decimals correctly, because you may only combine digits that share the same place value.
concepts.example: One idea will save you from many mistakes: a trailing zero does not change the value of a decimal. 0.3 and 0.30 are exactly the same amount, because three tenths equals thirty hundredths. That is why we are allowed to write extra zeros on the right whenever it helps us line numbers up. Be careful, though: a zero inside a number, like the 0 in 6.075, is doing an important job holding the tenths place empty, and you must never remove it.

concepts.title: Adding Decimal Numbers
concepts.explanation:
The golden rule of decimal addition is line up the decimal points. When the points are lined up vertically, tenths sit under tenths, hundredths under hundredths, and so on, so that you only ever add matching parts. If the numbers have different numbers of decimal places, add trailing zeros so every number has the same length. Then add from right to left, carrying whenever a column reaches ten, exactly as you do with whole numbers. Finally, bring the decimal point straight down into the answer.

Worked example: 4.49 + 3.09. Line up the points and add the hundredths first: 9 + 9 = 18, so write 8 and carry 1. Next the tenths: 4 + 0 + 1 carried = 5. Then the ones: 4 + 3 = 7. Bring the point down. The answer is 7.58. Estimate to check: 4 + 3 = 7, and 7.58 is close to 7, so the answer is reasonable.

Worked example with different lengths: 13.26 + 17.604. The first number has two decimal places and the second has three, so write 13.26 as 13.260 by adding one trailing zero. Now both have three places. Add thousandths: 0 + 4 = 4. Add hundredths: 6 + 0 = 6. Add tenths: 2 + 6 = 8. Add ones: 3 + 7 = 10, write 0 and carry 1. Add tens: 1 + 1 + 1 carried = 3. The answer is 30.864. Estimate: 13 + 18 = 31, which is close, so we can trust it.
concepts.example: Notice the habit forming here. You estimate first, you line up the points, you fill gaps with trailing zeros, you add right to left carrying when needed, and you check against the estimate at the end. Follow that same routine every single time and decimal addition becomes calm and reliable, even with long numbers.

concepts.title: Subtracting Decimal Numbers
concepts.explanation:
Subtracting decimals uses the same alignment as addition, but you must take extra care with borrowing, also called regrouping. Line up the points, add trailing zeros so both numbers have the same number of decimal places, then subtract from right to left. When a digit on top is too small to subtract from, borrow one from the place to its left, which is worth ten in the current column.

Worked example: 10.00 − 7.58. Write 10 as 10.00 so both numbers have two decimal places. Start at the hundredths: 0 − 8 will not go, so borrow. Working across the borrows, the tenths and ones lend down the line, and the calculation gives 2.42. Estimate to check: 10 − 8 = 2, and 2.42 is close to 2, so it is reasonable.

If borrowing across several zeros feels confusing, try the regrouping picture. Rewrite 10.00 as 9 + 0.9 + 0.10. Now subtract place by place: the ones give 9 − 7 = 2, the tenths give 0.9 − 0.5 = 0.4, and the hundredths give 0.10 − 0.08 = 0.02. Add the parts: 2 + 0.4 + 0.02 = 2.42. This shows exactly where the borrowed amounts came from and often makes the process feel far less mysterious.
concepts.example: Worked example with different lengths: 200.5 − 67.89. Write 200.5 as 200.50 so both have two decimal places. Subtract hundredths: 0 − 9 needs a borrow. Continue borrowing through the tenths, ones, tens and hundreds. The answer is 132.61. Estimate: 200 − 68 = 132, which matches closely, so we can trust the result.

concepts.title: Estimating to Check Decimals
concepts.explanation:
A good mathematician estimates before calculating. An estimate is a quick, sensible guess found by rounding each number to something easy, usually the nearest whole number. It is not the final answer; it is a guard that warns you if your careful calculation has gone badly wrong. If your worked answer is far from your estimate, stop and check for a misplaced decimal point or a lost trailing zero.

For example, to add 45.8 + 123.456 you might estimate 46 + 123 = 169. When your column method gives 169.256, the closeness tells you the answer is trustworthy. But if a slip had given you 16.9256 or 1692.56, the gap from 169 would shout that something is wrong. Estimation and exact calculation work together like two hands: one guesses, the other checks. Make estimating a habit and your accuracy will climb.
concepts.example: Estimation is especially powerful with money. Suppose Omar is buying goods costing 4.85, 9.20 and 6.95 shillings. Rounding each to the nearest whole gives 5 + 9 + 7 = 21, so he knows to expect a little over twenty shillings. If the till showed 210.00 or 2.10, he would spot instantly that a decimal point had jumped. This kind of quick mental guard protects you every day, long after you have left the classroom, whether you are checking a receipt, weighing produce, or measuring fuel. The more you practise rounding sensibly, the faster and sharper your estimates become.

concepts.title: Why Fractions Need a Common Denominator
concepts.explanation:
Adding and subtracting fractions is a little more thoughtful than working with whole numbers, because a fraction describes parts of a whole, and those parts can be different sizes. The denominator (bottom number) tells you into how many equal pieces one whole has been cut, and the numerator (top number) tells you how many of those pieces you have. You can only add or subtract fractions directly when the pieces are the same size, that is, when the denominators are equal.

Imagine adding 1/2 of a mango to 1/3 of a mango. A half is a bigger piece than a third, so you cannot simply add the numbers 1 and 1 and call it 2 of something, because the pieces do not match. To combine them fairly, you must cut both mangoes into the same number of equal pieces. This shared bottom number is called a common denominator, and finding it is the single most important skill in fraction addition and subtraction.
concepts.example: How do you find a common denominator? The most reliable way is the lowest common multiple (LCM) of the two denominators. List the multiples of each denominator and pick the smallest number that appears in both lists. For 1/4 and 1/6, the multiples of 4 are 4, 8, 12, 16, 20 and the multiples of 6 are 6, 12, 18, 24, so the LCM is 12. If you cannot spot the LCM quickly, you can always multiply the two denominators together (4 × 6 = 24); this always works, though the numbers may be larger than necessary and you may need to simplify at the end.

concepts.title: Adding and Subtracting Fractions
concepts.explanation:
Once both fractions share a common denominator, the work becomes straightforward: convert each fraction to an equivalent fraction with that denominator, then add or subtract only the numerators and keep the denominator the same. Finish by simplifying the answer and, if it is an improper fraction, changing it to a mixed number.

Worked example (addition): 2/5 + 3/4. The multiples of 5 are 5, 10, 15, 20 and the multiples of 4 are 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, so the common denominator is 20. Convert: 2/5 = (2×4)/(5×4) = 8/20, and 3/4 = (3×5)/(4×5) = 15/20. Add the numerators: 8/20 + 15/20 = 23/20. Since 23/20 is improper, convert it: 23/20 = 1 3/20. Check with decimals: 2/5 = 0.4 and 3/4 = 0.75, so the sum should be about 1.15, and 1 3/20 = 1.15. Correct!

Worked example (subtraction): 5/6 − 1/4. The multiples of 6 are 6, 12, 18 and the multiples of 4 are 4, 8, 12, so the common denominator is 12. Convert: 5/6 = 10/12 and 1/4 = 3/12. Subtract the numerators: 10/12 − 3/12 = 7/12. This cannot be simplified further. Check: 5/6 ≈ 0.83 and 1/4 = 0.25, and the difference is about 0.58, which matches 7/12 ≈ 0.58. Correct!
concepts.example: A very common error is to add the denominators as well as the numerators, writing 1/4 + 1/6 = 2/10. This is wrong, because the denominator tells you the size of the pieces, and the size does not change when you combine them; only the number of pieces changes. Always keep the common denominator the same and combine only the top numbers.

concepts.title: Adding and Subtracting Decimals Mentally
concepts.explanation: Not every decimal calculation needs a written column method. When the numbers are simple, you can often add or subtract decimals in your head by using place value and known number facts, the same way you already add and subtract whole numbers mentally. One strategy is to split a decimal into its whole-number part and its decimal part, deal with each part separately, then recombine them: to work out 3.6 + 2.5, add the whole numbers first (3 + 2 = 5), then add the decimal parts (0.6 + 0.5 = 1.1), then combine (5 + 1.1 = 6.1). Another strategy is to round one number to a nearby whole number, do the easier calculation, then adjust: to work out 4.9 + 3.6, treat 4.9 as 5 − 0.1, so 5 + 3.6 = 8.6, then subtract the 0.1 you added extra: 8.6 − 0.1 = 8.5. A third useful trick uses known whole-number facts: since you already know 7 + 8 = 15, you also instantly know 0.7 + 0.8 = 1.5 and 7 + 0.8 = 7.8, because the digits behave the same way regardless of where the decimal point sits — only the place value changes. These mental strategies are especially useful for checking that a written answer is reasonable, and for solving everyday problems, like adding prices, without needing pen and paper.
concepts.example: Use the split-and-recombine strategy to find 5.4 + 1.8 mentally. Whole numbers: 5 + 1 = 6. Decimal parts: 0.4 + 0.8 = 1.2. Combine: 6 + 1.2 = 7.2. Now use the round-and-adjust strategy to find 6.2 − 2.9 mentally: treat 2.9 as 3 − 0.1, so first work out 6.2 − 3 = 3.2, then add back the 0.1 you subtracted extra (because you subtracted 3 instead of 2.9, which is 0.1 too much): 3.2 + 0.1 = 3.3.

methods.title: How to add or subtract decimals
steps: Estimate the answer by rounding each number.
Write the numbers with points lined up; add trailing zeros so they match.
Work right to left, carrying (for adding) or borrowing (for subtracting).
Bring the decimal point straight down and check against your estimate.

methods.title: How to add or subtract fractions
steps: Find a common denominator (the lowest common multiple of the denominators).
Convert each fraction to an equivalent fraction with that denominator.
Add or subtract the numerators; keep the denominator the same.
Simplify, and change any improper fraction to a mixed number.

methods.title: How to subtract mixed numbers with borrowing
methods.example: Maryam buys items costing 12.75, 8.50 and 6.25 shillings. What is the total?
steps: Give both fractions a common denominator.
If the top fraction is smaller, borrow one whole (as denominator/denominator).
Subtract the whole numbers, then the fractions.
Or convert both to improper fractions to avoid borrowing entirely.

methods.title: Add fractions with different denominators
steps: Solution: The LCM of 3 and 6 is 6.
Convert: 1/3 = 2/6, and 1/6 stays as 1/6.
Add: 2/6 + 1/6 = 3/6 = 1/2 after simplifying.

methods.title: Subtract fractions
steps: Solution: Common denominator 6.
Convert: 2/3 = 4/6 and 1/6 stays.
Check with decimals: 0.67 − 0.17 = 0.5.

methods.title: Add mixed numbers
steps: Solution: Add wholes: 1 + 2 = 3.
Add fractions with denominator 4: 1/2 = 2/4, so 2/4 + 1/4 = 3/4.

workedExamples.title: Add decimals of different lengths
workedExamples.solution: Solution: Write 45.8 as 45.800 so both numbers have three decimal places. Estimate first: 46 + 123 = 169. Add right to left: thousandths 0+6=6; hundredths 0+5=5; tenths 8+4=12, write 2 carry 1; ones 5+3+1=9; tens 4+2=6; hundreds 0+1=1. Answer: 169.256, close to the estimate of 169. Correct.

workedExamples.title: Subtract across zeros
workedExamples.solution: Solution: Write 20 as 20.00. Estimate: 20 − 14 = 6. Subtract with borrowing: hundredths 0−5 borrow to give 5; tenths become 9−6=3; ones 9−3=6; tens 1−1=0. Answer: 6.35, close to the estimate of 6. Correct.

workedExamples.title: A shopping total
workedExamples.prompt: Maryam buys items costing 12.75, 8.50 and 6.25 shillings. What is the total?
workedExamples.solution: Solution: All have two decimal places, so line them up. 12.75 + 8.50 = 21.25, then 21.25 + 6.25 = 27.50 shillings. Estimate: 13 + 9 + 6 = 28, which confirms the answer.

workedExamples.title: Add fractions with different denominators
workedExamples.solution: Solution: The LCM of 3 and 6 is 6. Convert: 1/3 = 2/6, and 1/6 stays as 1/6. Add: 2/6 + 1/6 = 3/6 = 1/2 after simplifying. Check: 1/3 ≈ 0.33 and 1/6 ≈ 0.17, sum ≈ 0.5. Correct.

workedExamples.title: Subtract fractions
workedExamples.solution: Solution: Common denominator 6. Convert: 2/3 = 4/6 and 1/6 stays. Subtract: 4/6 − 1/6 = 3/6 = 1/2. Check with decimals: 0.67 − 0.17 = 0.5. Correct.

workedExamples.title: Add mixed numbers
workedExamples.solution: Solution: Add wholes: 1 + 2 = 3. Add fractions with denominator 4: 1/2 = 2/4, so 2/4 + 1/4 = 3/4. Combine: 3 + 3/4 = 3 3/4.

workedExamples.title: Subtract mixed numbers with borrowing
workedExamples.solution: Solution: Use a common denominator of 4: 3 1/2 = 3 2/4 and 1 3/4 stays. Since 2/4 is smaller than 3/4, borrow one whole: 3 2/4 becomes 2 6/4. Now subtract: wholes 2 − 1 = 1, fractions 6/4 − 3/4 = 3/4. Answer: 1 3/4. Check by improper fractions: 14/4 − 7/4 = 7/4 = 1 3/4. Correct.

workedExamples.title: A multi-step mixture
workedExamples.prompt: A tank holds 45.5 litres. First 12.75 litres is removed, then 8.25 litres is added. How much is in the tank now?
workedExamples.solution: Solution: Step 1: 45.5 − 12.75 = 32.75 litres. Step 2: 32.75 + 8.25 = 41.0 litres. Estimate: 46 − 13 + 8 = 41, which matches. Correct.

workedExamples.title: Find the missing amount
workedExamples.prompt: Hassan starts with 50.00 shillings. He spends 12.75, then 8.50, then 15.25. How much is left?
workedExamples.solution: Solution: Add the spending: 12.75 + 8.50 + 15.25 = 36.50. Then subtract from the start: 50.00 − 36.50 = 13.50 shillings. Estimate: 50 − 37 = 13, which confirms it.

workedExamples.title: Subtract mixed numbers with borrowing
workedExamples.prompt: Subtract mixed numbers with borrowing: a) 3 1/2 − 1 3/4 b) 3 1/4 − 1 2/3

activities.title: Market Receipt Challenge
activities.materials: paper, a pencil, and a few household items with pretend prices.
steps: Give five items 'shilling' prices with two decimal places, such as 3.45 and 12.80.
Choose any three items and add their prices, lining up the decimal points carefully.
Pretend to pay with a round note (for example 50.00) and work out the change by subtracting.
Ask a family member, your AI tutor, or a calculator to check your total and your change.
This trains the exact decimal skills you use every time you shop.

activities.title: Fraction Recipe Kitchen
activities.materials: a measuring cup (or a marked bottle) and water, rice or flour.
steps: Write a simple 'recipe' that uses fractions, such as 1/2 cup plus 1/3 cup.
Measure each amount, then work out the total by finding a common denominator.
Now pour some back and record how much is left as a subtraction of fractions.
Check your written answer against what you actually see in the cup.

activities.title: Decimal War (A Card Game)
activities.materials: number cards or slips of paper.
steps: Each player makes a decimal number with two places from three digit cards, such as 4.72.
Both players add their two most recent numbers; the larger total wins the round.
For a subtraction round, the larger number minus the smaller wins if the difference is over 1.
Keep score over ten rounds. Estimating quickly helps you decide who is ahead.
This game builds speed and confidence with lining up decimal points.
If you don't have another player available, deal two hands yourself and compare them, or play against your AI tutor.

activities.title: Jerrycan Water Investigation
activities.materials: a marked container and access to water (do this outside).
steps: Fill the container and record the starting amount as a decimal, such as 5.00 litres.
Pour some out for a task and measure what you removed, for example 1.75 litres.
Predict how much is left by subtracting, then measure to check your prediction.
Repeat with different amounts and see how close your predictions get each time.

activities.title: The Missing Number Puzzle (Family Game)
activities.materials: paper and pencil, and another person if available (or your AI tutor).
steps: One person writes an addition such as 4.5 + ___ = 7.2 and hides the missing number.
The other person (or your AI tutor, if playing alone) finds it by subtracting: 7.2 − 4.5 = 2.7.
Swap roles and try it with fractions, such as 3/4 + ___ = 1 whole.
Talk about how addition and subtraction undo each other.

activities.title: Rainfall Data Project (Investigation)
activities.materials: paper, and imagined or recorded daily amounts.
steps: Write down a decimal 'rainfall' amount in centimetres for each of five days.
Add all five amounts to find the weekly total, lining up the points.
Work out how far the total is above or below five 'average' days of 2.5 cm each.
Draw a simple bar for each day and label it with its decimal amount.

After your activities, talk or write about: Which activity helped you understand decimals or fractions best? What was the trickiest part, and how did you get past it? What would you like more practice with? Share your answers with your teacher at your next session.

rules.title: Decimal Alignment Rule
rules.text: Line up the decimal points, not the last digits. Fill gaps with trailing zeros so every number is the same length. Bring the decimal point straight down into the answer.

rules.title: Fraction Rule
rules.text: You can only add or subtract fractions with the same denominator. Find a common denominator (usually the lowest common multiple). Add or subtract the numerators only; keep the denominator the same; then simplify.

rules.title: Estimate-First Rule
rules.text: Round each number to a whole number and estimate before you calculate. If your exact answer is far from the estimate, check for a misplaced point.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: A bag of rice weighs 5 kg. Omar uses 1.35 kg, then 0.8 kg. How much is left?
Explain the key idea in Adding and Subtracting Fractions.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer:
Once both fractions share a common denominator, the work becomes straightforward: convert each fraction to an equivalent fraction with that denominator, then add or subtract only the numerators and keep the denominator the same. Finish by simplifying the answer and, if it is an improper fraction, changing it to a mixed number.

Worked example (addition): 2/5 + 3/4. The multiples of 5 are 5, 10, 15, 20 and the multiples of 4 are 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, so the common denominator is 20. Convert: 2/5 = (2×4)/(5×4) = 8/20, and 3/4 = (3×5)/(4×5) = 15/20. Add the numerators: 8/20 + 15/20 = 23/20. Since 23/20 is improper, convert it: 23/20 = 1 3/20. Check with decimals: 2/5 = 0.4 and 3/4 = 0.75, so the sum should be about 1.15, and 1 3/20 = 1.15. Correct!
